{{Short description|Type of space-filling polyhedron}}
In [[geometry]], a '''plesiohedron''' is a special kind of [[space-filling polyhedron]], defined as the [[Voronoi diagram|Voronoi cell]] of a symmetric [[Delone set]].
Three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] can be completely filled by copies of any one of these shapes, with no overlaps. The resulting [[honeycomb (geometry)|honeycomb]] will have symmetries that take any copy of the plesiohedron to any other copy.

The plesiohedra include the [[cube]], [[hexagonal prism]], [[rhombic dodecahedron]], and [[truncated octahedron]].
The largest number of faces that a plesiohedron can have is 38.

==Definition==
{{multiple image|image1=12-3 plesiohedron.png|width1=240|image2=12-3 plesioh-ani.gif|width2=190|footer=A 17-sided plesiohedron and its [[Honeycomb (geometry)|honeycomb]], the [[Voronoi diagram]] of the [[Laves graph]]}}
A set <math>S</math> of points in [[Euclidean space]] is a [[Delone set]] if there exists a number <math>\varepsilon>0</math> such that every two points of <math>S</math> are at least at distance <math>\varepsilon</math> apart from each other and such that every point of space is within distance <math>1/\varepsilon</math> of at least one point in <math>S</math>. So <math>S</math> fills space, but its points never come too close to each other. For this to be true, <math>S</math> must be infinite.
Additionally, the set <math>S</math> is symmetric (in the sense needed to define a plesiohedron) if, for every two points <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> of <math>S</math>, there exists a [[rigid motion]] of space that takes <math>S</math> to <math>S</math> and <math>p</math> to <math>q</math>. That is, the symmetries of <math>S</math> [[Group action (mathematics)|act transitively]] on <math>S</math>.<ref name="gs80"/>

The [[Voronoi diagram]] of any set <math>S</math> of points partitions space into regions called Voronoi cells that are nearer to one given point of <math>S</math> than to any other. When <math>S</math> is a Delone set, the Voronoi cell of each point <math>p</math> in <math>S</math> is a [[convex polyhedron]]. The faces of this polyhedron lie on the planes that perpendicularly bisect the line segments from <math>p</math> to other nearby points of <math>S</math>.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Aurenhammer | first = Franz | authorlink = Franz Aurenhammer
 | date = September 1991
 | doi = 10.1145/116873.116880
 | issue = 3
 | journal = [[ACM Computing Surveys]]
 | pages = 345–405
 | title = Voronoi diagrams—a survey of a fundamental geometric data structure
 | volume = 23}}. See especially section 1.2.1, "Regularly Placed Sites", pp.&nbsp;354–355.</ref>

When <math>S</math> is symmetric as well as being Delone, the Voronoi cells must all be [[Congruence (geometry)|congruent]] to each other, for the symmetries of <math>S</math> must also be symmetries of the Voronoi diagram. In this case, the Voronoi diagram forms a [[Honeycomb (geometry)|honeycomb]] in which there is only a single [[prototile]] shape, the shape of these Voronoi cells. This shape is called a plesiohedron. The tiling generated in this way is [[Isohedral tiling|isohedral]], meaning that it not only has a single prototile ("monohedral") but also that any copy of this tile can be taken to any other copy by a symmetry of the tiling.<ref name="gs80">{{citation
 | last1 = Grünbaum | first1 = Branko | author1-link = Branko Grünbaum
 | last2 = Shephard | first2 = G. C. | author2-link = Geoffrey Colin Shephard
 | doi = 10.1090/S0273-0979-1980-14827-2
 | issue = 3
 | journal = [[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]]
 | mr = 585178
 | pages = 951–973
 | series = New Series
 | title = Tilings with congruent tiles
 | volume = 3
 | year = 1980| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

As with any space-filling polyhedron, the [[Dehn invariant]] of a plesiohedron is necessarily zero.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Lagarias | first1 = J. C. | author1-link = Jeffrey Lagarias
 | last2 = Moews | first2 = D.
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02574064
 | issue = 3–4
 | journal = [[Discrete and Computational Geometry]]
 | mr = 1318797
 | pages = 573–583
 | title = Polytopes that fill <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> and scissors congruence
 | volume = 13
 | year = 1995| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

==Examples==
The plesiohedra include the five [[Parallelohedron|parallelohedra]]. These are polyhedra that can tile space in such a way that every tile is symmetric to every other tile by a translational symmetry, without rotation. Equivalently, they are the Voronoi cells of [[Lattice (group)|lattices]], as these are the translationally-symmetric Delone sets. Plesiohedra are a special case of the [[Stereohedron|stereohedra]], the prototiles of isohedral tilings more generally.<ref name="gs80"/> For this reason (and because Voronoi diagrams are also known as Dirichlet tesselations) they have also been called "Dirichlet stereohedra"<ref name="ss11"/>

There are only finitely many combinatorial types of plesiohedron. Notable individual plesiohedra include:
*The five parallelohedra: the [[cube]] (or more generally the [[parallelepiped]]), [[hexagonal prism]], [[rhombic dodecahedron]], [[elongated dodecahedron]], and [[truncated octahedron]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Erdahl | first = R. M.
 | doi = 10.1006/eujc.1999.0294
 | issue = 6
 | journal = European Journal of Combinatorics
 | mr = 1703597
 | pages = 527–549
 | title = Zonotopes, dicings, and Voronoi's conjecture on parallelohedra
 | volume = 20
 | year = 1999| doi-access = free
 }}. Voronoi conjectured that all tilings of higher dimensional spaces by translates of a single [[convex polytope]] are combinatorially equivalent to Voronoi tilings, and Erdahl proves this in the special case of [[zonotope]]s. But as he writes (p.&nbsp;429), Voronoi's conjecture for dimensions at most four was already proven by Delaunay. For the classification of three-dimensional parallelohedra into these five types, see {{harvtxt|Grünbaum|Shephard|1980}}.</ref>
*The [[triangular prism]], the prototile of the [[triangular prismatic honeycomb]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Pugh | first = Anthony
 | contribution = Close-packing polyhedra
 | contribution-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=IDDxpYQTR7kC&pg=PA48
 | mr = 0451161
 | pages = 48–50
 | publisher = University of California Press, Berkeley, Calif.-London
 | title = Polyhedra: a visual approach
 | year = 1976}}.</ref> More generally, each of the 11 types of [[Laves tiling]] of the plane by congruent convex polygons (and each of the subtypes of these tilings with different symmetry groups) can be realized as the Voronoi cells of a symmetric Delone set in the plane.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Delone | first1 = B. N. | author1-link = Boris Delaunay
 | last2 = Dolbilin | first2 = N. P.
 | last3 = Štogrin | first3 = M. I.
 | journal = Trudy Matematicheskogo Instituta imeni V. A. Steklova
 | mr = 558946
 | pages = 109–140, 275
 | title = Combinatorial and metric theory of planigons
 | volume = 148
 | year = 1978}}.</ref> It follows that the prisms over each of these shapes are plesiohedra. As well as the triangular prisms, these include prisms over certain quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons.
*The [[gyrobifastigium]] is a stereohedron but not a plesiohedron, because the points at the centers of the cells of its face-to-face tiling (where they are forced to go by symmetry) have differently-shaped Voronoi cells. However, a flattened version of the gyrobifastigium, with faces made of [[isosceles right triangle]]s and [[silver rectangle]]s, is a plesiohedron.
*The [[triakis truncated tetrahedron]], the prototile of the [[triakis truncated tetrahedral honeycomb]] and the plesiohedron generated by the [[diamond lattice]]<ref name="gs80"/>
*The [[trapezo-rhombic dodecahedron]], the prototile of the [[trapezo-rhombic dodecahedral honeycomb]] and the plesiohedron generated by the [[Close-packing of equal spheres|hexagonal close-packing]]<ref name="lagarias">{{citation
 | last = Lagarias | first = Jeffrey C.
 | contribution = The Kepler conjecture and its proof
 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4614-1129-1_1
 | mr = 3050907
 | publisher = Springer, New York
 | title = The Kepler Conjecture: The Hales–Ferguson proof
 | year = 2011| isbn = 978-1-4614-1128-4
 | page = 11
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=qKNAHyQQcssC&pg=PA11
}}</ref>
*The 17-sided Voronoi cells of the [[Laves graph]]<ref>{{citation
 | last = Schoen | first = Alan H.
 | date = June–July 2008
 | issue = 6
 | journal = [[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]
 | page = 663
 | title = On the graph (10,3)-a
 | url = https://www.ams.org/notices/200806/tx080600663p.pdf
 | volume = 55}}.</ref>
Many other plesiohedra are known. Two different ones with the largest known number of faces, 38, were discovered by crystallographer Peter Engel.<ref name="gs80"/><ref>{{citation
 | last = Engel | first = Peter
 | doi = 10.1524/zkri.1981.154.3-4.199
 | issue = 3–4
 | journal = Zeitschrift für Kristallographie, Kristallgeometrie, Kristallphysik, Kristallchemie
 | mr = 598811
 | pages = 199–215
 | title = Über Wirkungsbereichsteilungen von kubischer Symmetrie
 | volume = 154
 | year = 1981| bibcode = 1981ZK....154..199E
 }}.</ref> 
For many years, the maximum number of faces of a plesiohedron was an [[open problem]],<ref>{{citation
 | last = Shephard | first = G. C. | authorlink = Geoffrey Colin Shephard
 | doi = 10.2307/3616930
 | issue = 448
 | pages = 117–120 | journal = [[The Mathematical Gazette]]
 | title = 69.14 Space Filling with Identical Symmetrical Solids
 | volume = 69
 | year = 1985| jstor = 3616930 }}.</ref><ref name="ss11">{{citation
 | last1 = Sabariego | first1 = Pilar
 | last2 = Santos | first2 = Francisco | author2-link = Francisco Santos Leal
 | doi = 10.1007/s13366-011-0010-5
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Beiträge zur Algebra und Geometrie
 | mr = 2842627
 | pages = 237–263
 | title = On the number of facets of three-dimensional Dirichlet stereohedra IV: quarter cubic groups
 | volume = 52
 | year = 2011| arxiv = 0708.2114}}.</ref>
but analysis of the possible symmetries of three-dimensional space has shown that this number is at most 38.<ref name=schmitt/>

The Voronoi cells of points uniformly spaced on a [[helix]] fill space, are all congruent to each other, and can be made to have arbitrarily large numbers of faces.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Erickson | first1 = Jeff
 | last2 = Kim | first2 = Scott | author2-link = Scott Kim
 | arxiv = math/0106095
 | contribution = Arbitrarily large neighborly families of congruent symmetric convex 3-polytopes
 | mr = 2034721
 | pages = 267–278
 | publisher = Dekker, New York
 | series = Monogr. Textbooks Pure Appl. Math.
 | title = Discrete geometry
 | volume = 253
 | year = 2003| bibcode = 2001math......6095E}}.</ref> However, the points on a helix are not a Delone set and their Voronoi cells are not bounded polyhedra.

A modern survey is given by Schmitt.<ref name=schmitt>{{citation
 | last1 = Schmitt | first1 = Moritz
 | title = On Space Groups and Dirichlet-Voronoi Stereohedra
 | url = https://refubium.fu-berlin.de/handle/fub188/10176
 | year = 2016
 | doi = 10.17169/refubium-14374
 }}.</ref>
